ocar.opportunity: Connectomics can map cells and synapses at nanometer scale, but typical reconstructed volumes of about 1 mm³ are smaller than human cerebral cortex, which can be 3 mm thick. Fresh cortical biopsies taken during deep-brain-stimulation lead placement offer a path to synapse-level maps from patients with psychiatric and neurologic disorders.
ocar.challenge: Larger human circuit reconstructions are limited by access to fresh biopsies, the need to preserve ultrastructure including extracellular space, and the requirement for uniform heavy-metal staining throughout the block. Perfusion with fixative is not possible in these neurosurgical samples.
ocar.action: Karlupia, Schalek, Wu, Meirovitch, Wei, Charney, Kopell, and Lichtman report in Biological Psychiatry (2023) an immersion-fixation, osmium staining, and processing protocol optimized empirically across 147 protocol variables in 237 samples. Principles include transfer of biopsies to fixative within 5 minutes, cool temperatures, mannitol to preserve extracellular space, extensive washing, CaCl₂ to reduce membrane breaks, and adjusted thiocarbohydrazide and osmium timings.
ocar.resolution: The method consistently gave excellent ultrastructure throughout human and rodent surgical brain samples of 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ and of volumes up to 37 mm³ with one dimension ≤ 2 mm. Rapid cold immersion preserved labile features such as dendritic spinules, astrocytic glycogen granules, unusual vascular invaginations, and presynaptic omega figures. Mouse volumes were automatically segmented; human volumes were manually segmented and aligned for multibeam imaging.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the protocol as enabling synapse-level circuit analysis in psychiatric and neurologic patient biopsies; applying it to full-thickness cortical reconstructions in disease cohorts is the implied next use.

summaries.beginner: Human brain samples for electron microscopy usually cannot be perfused with fixative the way animal brains can. This team shows how to dunk fresh surgical biopsies in cold fixative and stain them so large chunks stay well preserved for mapping synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In Biological Psychiatry (2023), Karlupia and colleagues describe immersion fixation and heavy-metal staining for multi-cubic-millimeter human and rodent surgical samples destined for EM connectomics. After testing 147 protocol variables on 237 samples, they report excellent ultrastructure in 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ blocks and in volumes up to 37 mm³ provided one dimension is ≤ 2 mm. Mannitol-aided extracellular-space preservation and CaCl₂ membrane stabilization are highlighted as practical keys, together with fast (≤5 min) transfer of fresh tissue. Human cortex came from DBS lead-placement biopsies; aligned multibeam EM and mixed manual/automatic segmentation are used to demonstrate tracing-ready quality.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper on sample preparation, not a completed human connectome. Volume claims specify geometry (2 mm cubes; up to 37 mm³ with one dimension ≤ 2 mm) rather than a full 3 mm cortical column in every case. Protocol optimization was empirical across many variables; underlying osmium chemistry remains partly uncertain, as the authors note. Human tissue is neurosurgical, not population-normal. Dataset tags pointing at MICrONS in the catalog should not be read as this paper reconstructing that mouse volume.

plain_language_summary: Human brain samples for electron microscopy usually cannot be perfused with fixative the way animal brains can. This team shows how to dunk fresh surgical biopsies in cold fixative and stain them so large chunks stay well preserved for mapping synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron type is central to reading a connectome and to studying neurological disease, but anatomical, physiological, and molecular typing are slow and expensive. Volume electron microscopy now supplies high-resolution morphology and connectivity together, which could support automated classification if models used both sources.
ocar.challenge: Few models are built for automated neuron classification from whole-brain connectomes that jointly encode skeleton morphology and circuit topology. Skeleton point clouds and connectivity graphs are permutation-sensitive representations, so encoders must be invariant to arbitrary point and node order.
ocar.action: Liao, Wan, and Du propose NeuNet (arXiv 2023 / AAAI), with a Skeleton Encoder that applies one-dimensional convolution to skeleton points in a bottom-up fashion, a Connectome Encoder that uses a graph neural network on the circuit, and a Readout Layer that fuses the two for classification. They reprocess and release two neuron-classification datasets from volume EM of human brain cortex and Drosophila brain.
ocar.resolution: On those two datasets NeuNet reached accuracies of 0.9169 (human cortex) and 0.9363 (Drosophila brain) and outperformed other baseline models in the paper. Code and data are released at a public GitHub repository.
ocar.future_work: The authors position NeuNet as a framework for connectome-based typing; testing on additional species, finer type catalogs, and noisier automatic reconstructions is the natural extension.

summaries.beginner: A neuron’s identity is written both in its 3D shape and in who it talks to. This paper trains a computer to use both the stick-figure skeleton and the wiring diagram to guess each cell’s type.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2023) as an AAAI paper, Liao, Wan, and Du introduce NeuNet, which jointly encodes neuronal skeletons and circuit topology with permutation-invariant encoders. A 1D convolution over skeleton points captures morphology; a GNN captures connectome structure; a readout fuses both for classification. They reprocess volume-EM reconstructions of human cortex and Drosophila brain into two public classification datasets, reporting accuracies of 0.9169 and 0.9363 respectively, above the paper’s baselines.
summaries.advanced: Accuracies are reported as two scalars without class-wise scores, confusion matrices, or reconstruction-error rates in the extracted text. “Whole-brain connectome” in the abstract should not be read as a newly imaged complete human brain; the human set is cortex volume EM. Permutation-invariance is proven for a restricted Conv1D setting (kernel size 1, stride 1). Type granularity and how labels were obtained from the source reconstructions are not specified here.

plain_language_summary: A neuron’s identity is written both in its 3D shape and in who it talks to. This paper trains a computer to use both the stick-figure skeleton and the wiring diagram to guess each cell’s type.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstructions from volume EM have gained from ever more precise automatic segmentation, but neuroscience still needs user-friendly open tools so labs can train networks and proofread without writing code or renting clusters.
ocar.challenge: State-of-the-art 3D convolutional pipelines often assume high-end compute. MATLAB users tracing on ordinary desktops lack an interactive wrapper that covers ground-truth labeling, preprocessing, training, and on-the-fly prediction while remaining compatible with existing annotation software.
ocar.action: Pavarino, Yang, Dhanyasi, and colleagues present mEMbrain in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2023): a MATLAB tool, integrated as an API to VAST, for Linux and Windows commodity desktops. It wraps ground-truth generation, image preprocessing, deep-network training, and on-the-fly predictions for proofreading. They tested it on datasets spanning species, scales, nervous-system regions, and developmental stages.
ocar.resolution: The authors release an EM ground-truth resource from four animals and five datasets, about 180 hours of expert annotation totaling more than 1.2 GB of labeled images, plus four pretrained networks. Software and resources are posted at the Lichtman lab mEMbrain site, with the goal of lab-based reconstructions that do not require user coding.
ocar.future_work: A hoped-for later edition would train state-of-the-art 3D CNNs such as 3C; the current tool emphasizes 2D section segmentation, which the authors say can still be satisfactory depending on staining and alignment.

summaries.beginner: Tracing neurons in electron-microscope pictures usually needs expert programmers and big computers. This free MATLAB add-on lets a lab label examples, train a network, and check predictions on an ordinary desktop, using software many biologists already know.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2023), Pavarino, Yang, Meirovitch, Lichtman and colleagues introduce mEMbrain, an interactive MATLAB segmentation tool wired into VAST. It covers ground-truth generation, preprocessing, network training, and on-the-fly proofreading on Linux or Windows commodity machines. Tests span multiple species and scales. They release ~180 hours of expert labels from four animals and five datasets (>1.2 GB) and four pretrained networks, arguing that abolishing cluster costs makes connectomics more affordable.
summaries.advanced: Affordable connectomics here means local 2D CNN workflows, not a claim of matching petascale 3D pipelines. The authors themselves flag 3D CNNs as future work and note that 2D section results depend on stain quality and alignment. Annotation hours and GB of labels quantify the released resource, not reconstruction completeness of any one volume. Species coverage is described as diverse but not fully enumerated in the extracted text.

plain_language_summary: Tracing neurons in electron-microscope pictures usually needs expert programmers and big computers. This free MATLAB add-on lets a lab label examples, train a network, and check predictions on an ordinary desktop, using software many biologists already know.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can reconstruct synaptic networks but lacks the molecular labels that identify cell types and functional properties. Volumetric correlated light and electron microscopy (vCLEM) can overlay fluorescence on the same EM volume if probes penetrate without detergents that ruin ultrastructure.
ocar.challenge: Conventional antibodies are large and usually need detergents, which conflict with EM preservation. Multiplexed molecular contrast on a single connectomic sample therefore requires smaller probes that still bind useful markers.
ocar.action: Han, Lu, Li, Wang, Schalek, Meirovitch, Lichtman, Trimmer and colleagues (Research Square, 2023) generated eight fluorescent single-chain variable fragment (scFv) immuno-probes against GFP, GFAP, calbindin, parvalbumin, Kv1.2 (KCNA2), VGLUT1, PSD-95, and neuropeptide Y. They performed detergent-free multiplexed labeling, confocal imaging with spectral unmixing, then ssEM on the same mouse cerebellar Crus I sample, depositing plasmids at Addgene.
ocar.resolution: Six probes were imaged together with excellent ultrastructure and superimposed fluorescence channels. The volume documented a poorly described cerebellar cell type, two types of mossy-fiber terminals, and subcellular localization of one ion-channel type. Usable vCLEM volumes reached 120 μm depth; scFv conversion from NeuroMab monoclonal antibodies is reported at about 50%. A version of record later appeared in Nature Communications (2024).
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that because scFvs can be derived from existing monoclonal antibodies, hundreds of probes could be generated; they discuss conversion strategies, combinatorial cell typing, and combining scFv labeling with calcium or voltage imaging.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope maps show every wire but not which molecular “name tags” a cell carries. This team makes tiny fluorescent antibody pieces that soak into tissue without soap, so the same mouse cerebellum chunk can be seen in color and then in EM detail.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on Research Square (2023), Han, Lichtman, Trimmer and colleagues introduce detergent-free scFv immuno-probes for multiplexed volumetric CLEM. Eight fluorescent scFvs target GFP, GFAP, calbindin, parvalbumin, Kv1.2, VGLUT1, PSD-95, and NPY; six were unmixed by confocal microscopy on mouse cerebellar Crus I and followed by serial-section EM. They report excellent ultrastructure with registered fluorescence, a poorly described cerebellar cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, ion-channel subcellular localization, and ~120 μm usable depth. Expression plasmids are deposited at Addgene.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-and-cytology preprint (later Nature Communications 2024); “hundreds of probes” is a projection from monoclonal libraries, not a count delivered here. Conversion success is ~50% for the NeuroMab recombinant subset attempted. Six-color unmixing is not an upper bound—the discussion cites published 45-color linear unmixing and Raman dyes as possible extensions, not results of this experiment. Depth is limited by confocal imaging of uncleared tissue even though scFvs penetrate further.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope maps show every wire but not which molecular “name tags” a cell carries. This team makes tiny fluorescent antibody pieces that soak into tissue without soap, so the same mouse cerebellum chunk can be seen in color and then in EM detail.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM connectomics volumes now surpass 1 mm³, packing dense multi-scale structure that cannot be annotated synapse-by-synapse by hand. Compact vector representations of segmented synapses could speed proofreading, similarity search, and imputation of labels.
ocar.challenge: Manual inspection of individual synapses takes years at this scale. Supervised models need many labels, and human-designed features may miss both biological subtype structure and technical segmentation artifacts.
ocar.action: Wilson and Babadi present SynapseCLR in Patterns (2023), a self-supervised contrastive method adapted from SimCLR to segmented 3D EM objects, applied to synapses in mouse primary visual cortex. Representations are used for one-shot detection of defective segmentations, dataset-wide similarity queries, and imputation of annotations from a small labeled subset.
ocar.resolution: Feature representations separated synapses by appearance and by functionally important structural annotations. Excitatory versus inhibitory neuronal types could be assigned with >99.8% accuracy to individual synapses and highly truncated neurites after ensembling, using manual annotation of only 0.2% of the dataset’s synapses. Unsupervised analysis of the representation manifold revealed intrinsic axes of variation, including cleft size and mitochondrial pattern for E-to-E synapses, and evidence of inhibitory subtype information.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for applying the same unsupervised representations to other organelles and to linking synaptic structure with microcircuit identity as EM volumes grow.

summaries.beginner: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged in 3D contains far too many synapses for people to label one by one. This method teaches a computer to compare synapse snapshots with no labels, then uses a tiny handful of human tags to fill in the rest and to flag broken reconstructions.
summaries.intermediate: In Patterns (2023), Wilson and Babadi introduce SynapseCLR, a SimCLR-style contrastive learner for segmented 3D EM objects, demonstrated on mouse visual-cortex synapses. Representations separate synapses by appearance and structural annotations, support one-shot identification of defective segmentations, and impute labels from 0.2% manual annotation. Excitatory versus inhibitory assignment exceeds 99.8% accuracy at the synapse and, after ensembling, on highly truncated neurites. UMAP axes include cleft size and mitochondrial presence for E-to-E synapses.
summaries.advanced: The >99.8% figure is for E versus I assignment on this mouse visual-cortex volume, not a universal synapse-type accuracy. Ensembling over neurites is what rescues truncated fragments. Defective-segmentation detection is few-shot, not a published merge/split path-length benchmark against all competing agglomeration methods. Inhibitory subtype information is described as suggested by the manifold, not as a fully validated classifier. Augmentations include blanked sections; representations were insensitive to the number of missing sections in controls.

plain_language_summary: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged in 3D contains far too many synapses for people to label one by one. This method teaches a computer to compare synapse snapshots with no labels, then uses a tiny handful of human tags to fill in the rest and to flag broken reconstructions.

ocar.opportunity: The synaptic map of a circuit constrains what computations it can perform, so inferring generative design principles of connectomes would link development, architecture, learning, and behavior. Complementary local wiring rules and global network statistics have rarely been learned in one model.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear how far large-scale organization can be explained by simple local connectivity rules, or how small-world and modular patterns would emerge from those rules. Any one measured connectome is also a noisy outcome of genetics, development, and learning, so models must be probabilistic.
ocar.action: Haber, Wanner, Friedrich, and Schneidman (bioRxiv 2023) learn probabilistic generative models for the zebrafish olfactory bulb, part of mouse visual cortex, and C. elegans, using a small number of simple biological and physical features as building blocks. They also simulate synthetic zebrafish olfactory-bulb circuits and add latent features where base models fail.
ocar.resolution: In all three systems the compact models accurately predicted individual synapses and their strength, in- and out-degree distributions, subnetwork motif frequencies, and other properties. Synthetic olfactory-bulb circuits replicated the computation the real circuit performs in response to olfactory cues. Specific failures of the models pointed to missing design features that latent variables then uncovered.
ocar.future_work: Natural extensions include models of connectome development over time, populations of animals, and adding explicit computational goals so structure–function links can be studied in biological and artificial networks.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring looks complicated, but much of it may follow a few simple local rules. This study builds statistical models of three very different circuits and finds that those simple ingredients already predict both the wiring and, in one case, the circuit’s job.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Haber, Wanner, Friedrich, and Schneidman fit probabilistic generative models to connectomes of the zebrafish olfactory bulb, a portion of mouse visual cortex, and C. elegans. Models using a small set of biological and physical features predicted synapses and strengths, degree distributions, and motif frequencies. Synthetic zebrafish olfactory-bulb networks generated by the model reproduced odor-evoked computation measured in the real circuit. Residual errors were interpreted by adding latent features that capture missing design principles.
summaries.advanced: “Highly accurate” is not given as a single numeric score in the extracted text; claims cover multiple structural statistics rather than a held-out whole-brain test. Functional replication is reported for the zebrafish olfactory bulb, not for mouse cortex or C. elegans in this preprint. Connectomes are treated as snapshots; developmental time series are proposed, not fit. Stochasticity of individual brains means model error is partly bounded by animal-to-animal variability, as the authors note.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring looks complicated, but much of it may follow a few simple local rules. This study builds statistical models of three very different circuits and finds that those simple ingredients already predict both the wiring and, in one case, the circuit’s job.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can map local mammalian circuits but does not currently scale to a whole mouse brain, leaving long-range projections unmapped. X-ray holographic nanotomography (XNH) can image brain tissue at larger scale and is well suited to thick myelinated axons that carry most inter-region communication, offering a route to brain-wide projectomics.
ocar.challenge: XNH volumes are typically lower resolution and larger field-of-view than EM, so accurate axon segmentation remains an open problem. Dense voxel-wise ground truth is slow to paint, which bottlenecks training of segmentation networks, whereas skeletons that follow axon trajectories are faster to annotate and already determine connectivity.
ocar.action: Nguyen, Narwani, Larson, Li, Xie, Pfister, Wei, Shavit, Mi, Pacureanu, Lee, and Kuan introduce the XPRESS challenge (arXiv 2023): volumetric XNH images of mouse cortical white-matter axons with ground-truth axon trajectories. They provide a small volume of voxel-wise labels and a larger volume of skeleton annotations, and they encourage methods that train from skeletons.
ocar.resolution: The challenge defines evaluation as how accurately submitted segmentations agree with ground-truth skeleton annotations, framing skeleton-supervised segmentation as the practical path to XNH projectomes.
ocar.future_work: The organizers present XPRESS as a community benchmark; successful skeleton-trained methods would be the next step toward brain-wide myelinated-projection maps.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can see every synapse locally but cannot yet photograph a whole mouse brain. This contest shares X-ray nanotomography pictures of white-matter cables and asks computers to trace those axons, using stick-figure drawings as the main teaching signal.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2023), Nguyen, Kuan, Lee, Pacureanu and colleagues present XPRESS (X-ray Projectomic Reconstruction — Extracting Segmentation with Skeletons). The task is axon instance segmentation in synchrotron XNH volumes of mouse cortical white matter, which the authors argue can scale toward brain-wide projectomes of myelinated tracts. Training resources include a small densely voxel-labeled volume and a larger skeleton-annotated volume; submissions are scored against skeleton ground truth.
summaries.advanced: This is a challenge description, not a leaderboard of finished algorithms or a completed mouse projectome. XNH is described as slightly lower resolution than EM and as especially suited to thick myelinated axons, not to synaptic neuropil. No numeric resolution, volume size, or baseline scores appear in the extracted text. “We demonstrated” XNH for larger-scale imaging refers to prior work by the organizers, not new whole-brain data in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can see every synapse locally but cannot yet photograph a whole mouse brain. This contest shares X-ray nanotomography pictures of white-matter cables and asks computers to trace those axons, using stick-figure drawings as the main teaching signal.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale synapse-resolution reconstructions now let neuroscientists search for small repeating subgraphs thought to be circuit building blocks. Finding those motifs only in the graph is not enough: each instance must be mapped back onto 3D neuron and synapse morphology.
ocar.challenge: Motifs are typically only 2–6 neurons, but connectomes are huge and morphologically tangled, so search, review, and visual comparison are hard. Non-graph-experts also need a way to sketch queries rather than write graph algorithms. Motif chains, in which a motif repeats 2–4 times, add another layer of structure.
ocar.action: Troidl, Warchol, Choi, Matelsky, Dhanyasi, Wang, Wester, Wei, Lichtman, Pfister, and Beyer present Vimo on bioRxiv (2023): an interactive visual system to sketch motifs, constrain neuron and synapse properties, query large connectomes, and inspect motif instances in 3D. A continuous focus-and-context design prunes unrelated branches and uses exploded views with hierarchical synapse clustering and bundling. They evaluate with a user study and a case study of seven domain experts on FlyEM Hemibrain.
ocar.resolution: On a fruit-fly connectome with more than 21,000 neurons and 20 million synapses, experts could generate and confirm hypotheses through fast analysis iterations and connectivity highlighting. The system is demonstrated on Hemibrain data (Scheffer et al.).
ocar.future_work: The work is a visualization design study; extending motif-chain analysis and the same interaction model to other proofread connectomes is the implied next use.

summaries.beginner: When a wiring diagram has tens of thousands of cells, looking for a repeating little circuit is like finding a pattern in a huge subway map. This software lets scientists draw the pattern, jump to every match, and peel the 3D cells apart so the connections are easier to see.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Troidl, Beyer, Pfister and colleagues introduce Vimo for visual analysis of neuronal connectivity motifs and motif chains. Users sketch 2–6 neuron motifs, filter by structural properties, and inspect instances in 3D with focus-and-context pruning and exploded synapse-bundled views. A user study and an in-depth case study with seven domain experts used the FlyEM Hemibrain, with more than 21,000 neurons and 20 million synapses. The authors report that the tool supports fast hypothesis generation and confirmation.
summaries.advanced: Evaluation is a qualitative design study with seven experts, not a timed motif-finding benchmark against graph databases. Motif-size ranges (2–6 neurons; chains 2–4 repeats) are design targets, not completeness claims for all biologically relevant subgraphs. Hemibrain is a partial adult fly brain; the introduction also cites H01 human cortex as a scale example, not as data analyzed here. The title uses ViMO; the paper text uses Vimo.

plain_language_summary: When a wiring diagram has tens of thousands of cells, looking for a repeating little circuit is like finding a pattern in a huge subway map. This software lets scientists draw the pattern, jump to every match, and peel the 3D cells apart so the connections are easier to see.

ocar.opportunity: Wiring architecture is assumed to strongly determine a network’s dynamics, so pairing a complete synapse-resolution connectome with brain-wide activity should reveal how anatomy supports global computations. C. elegans uniquely offers both maps in one compact nervous system.
ocar.challenge: How the anatomical connectome and neuronal dynamics relate on a global scale remains unsolved. Local synapse counts that seem intuitively important may not be the graph features that actually predict functional relationships.
ocar.action: Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer in Current Biology (2022) systematically compare graph features in the C. elegans connectome with correlations in nervous-system-wide neuronal dynamics. They evaluate local motifs versus non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarity, and they test whether connection strength or amount of common input improves predictions. They then inhibit hub neurons to test effects on brain-wide correlations.
ocar.resolution: Few local connectivity motifs, and mostly non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarities, predicted functional relationships. Connection strength and amount of common inputs did not improve those predictions, suggesting that topology is sufficient. Hub neurons are key to the relevant graph features; inhibiting multiple hub neurons specifically disrupted brain-wide correlations.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose that a set of hub neurons plus non-local connectivity features provide an anatomical substrate for global brain dynamics; causal tests of additional hubs and finer dynamical timescales are natural follow-ups.

summaries.beginner: In a tiny worm, scientists can compare the full wiring diagram with how cells fire together across the whole brain. This paper finds that a few well-connected hub cells, and patterns that reach beyond simple neighbor links, help explain those brain-wide activity partnerships.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Biology (2022), Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer compare C. elegans connectome graph features with correlations in brain-wide neuronal dynamics. Non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarity predicted functional relationships better than most local motifs. Adding connection strength or the amount of common input did not improve predictions. Hub neurons concentrated the relevant features, and inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupted brain-wide correlations.
summaries.advanced: The extracted PDF body for this record is a different paper (Portman et al. on sexual dimorphism); pedagogical text therefore follows the bibliographic abstract only. No numeric prediction scores, hub identities, or animal counts appear in that abstract. “Topology is sufficient” is restricted to the features tested against the reported activity correlations. Inhibition of multiple hubs is described as specific disruption of brain-wide correlations, not as a full circuit-breaking map.

plain_language_summary: In a tiny worm, scientists can compare the full wiring diagram with how cells fire together across the whole brain. This paper finds that a few well-connected hub cells, and patterns that reach beyond simple neighbor links, help explain those brain-wide activity partnerships.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution connectomics now produces cubic-millimeter-scale volumes with tens of thousands of cells and hundreds of millions of synapses, so neuroscientists need visualization at every pipeline step—from acquisition through segmentation, proofreading, exploration, and circuit analysis.
ocar.challenge: These datasets are too large and tangled to understand from static figures. Visualization research is unevenly distributed along the pipeline, and newcomers lack a map of open tools and public datasets.
ocar.action: Beyer, Troidl, Boorboor, Hadwiger, Kaufman, and Pfister publish a EuroVis state-of-the-art report in Computer Graphics Forum (2022) surveying visualization methods across the connectomics pipeline. They define pipeline stages, review how visualization is integrated in each, and compile open-science resources including open-source tools and publicly available datasets.
ocar.resolution: The survey groups work along acquisition, segmentation, proofreading, interactive exploration, and circuit analysis, noting that most visualization research clusters toward the end of the pipeline while earlier stages also have notable methods (for example interactive image-quality assessment during acquisition). They argue that human–AI collaboration will grow as imaging data explode, and they highlight interdisciplinarity among neuroscientists, machine-learning experts, and visualization researchers.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope the report inspires new visualization research on remaining challenges, toward the long-term goal of interpreting human-scale wiring.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps from electron microscopes are so big that scientists need clever pictures and interactive tools just to work with them. This review walks through those tools from the moment images are taken to the moment circuits are analyzed, and lists free datasets and software.
summaries.intermediate: In Computer Graphics Forum (2022), Beyer, Troidl and colleagues present a EuroVis STAR on visualization and analysis in high-resolution connectomics. They structure the literature along the pipeline from high-resolution acquisition through automated segmentation, proofreading, interactive exploration, and circuit analysis, and they survey open-source tools and public datasets. They note that visualization is already used for acquisition quality control and proofreading, that most published vis systems sit downstream, and that open sharing is essential in this interdisciplinary field.
summaries.advanced: This is a survey, not a new algorithm or dataset. Cubic-millimeter feasibility is attributed to cited imaging and segmentation papers, not demonstrated here. Tool and dataset tables will age. The “ultimate goal” of a complete human connectome is stated as field aspiration, not a claim that such a map exists.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps from electron microscopes are so big that scientists need clever pictures and interactive tools just to work with them. This review walks through those tools from the moment images are taken to the moment circuits are analyzed, and lists free datasets and software.

ocar.opportunity: Large volumetric EM reconstructions can reveal hidden cerebellar connectivity, but synapse detection has lagged behind neuron reconstruction. Once neuronal fragments can be typed, contacts between them become a structured classification problem rather than a raw-image search.
ocar.challenge: Generic synapse detectors often demand heavy retraining and still struggle with tissue-specific geometry. Cerebellar molecular-layer circuits have stereotyped cell types and type connectivity that general methods do not exploit.
ocar.action: Park, Gim, Lee, Lee, and Kim in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2022) automatically detect synapses in 3D EM of the mouse cerebellar molecular layer (CML). They extract contacts between reconstructed, type-identified fragments and classify them as synaptic or not using type information plus two deep-learning models, then assign pre/post sides and excitatory versus inhibitory type.
ocar.resolution: Accuracy is estimated at 0.955 F1-score on a CML test volume containing 508 synapses. As a usability demonstration they measured synapse size and number and inspected subcellular connectivity among CML fragments. Processing the test set took less than 20 minutes on a desktop with 8 CPU cores and 32 GB memory.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that exploiting tissue-specific properties can extend to other regions if cell types and type connectivity are well defined, with new networks, training data, and type-restriction policies as needed.

summaries.beginner: Finding every synapse in a 3D brain picture is still harder than tracing the cells. This method looks at touching pieces of known cerebellar cell types and asks two computer networks whether each touch is a real synapse, and whether it is excitatory or inhibitory.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2022), Park and Kim and colleagues present a cerebellum-specific synapse detector for mouse molecular-layer EM. Contacts between reconstructed, typed neuronal fragments are classified with type constraints and two deep networks, including assignment of polarity and E/I class. They report an F1-score of 0.955 on a test volume with 508 synapses, then quantify synapse size, number, and subcellular connectivity. Runtime on the test set is under 20 minutes on an 8-core, 32 GB desktop.
summaries.advanced: High accuracy is reported for one CML test volume of 508 synapses, not a multi-region bakeoff. The method is explicitly tweaked for cerebellum and identified fragment types; the authors list architecture changes, retraining, and well-defined type connectivity as requirements for transfer. Comparison to newer generally usable AI packages is discussed as an ongoing community need rather than a head-to-head table in the extracted text.

plain_language_summary: Finding every synapse in a 3D brain picture is still harder than tracing the cells. This method looks at touching pieces of known cerebellar cell types and asks two computer networks whether each touch is a real synapse, and whether it is excitatory or inhibitory.

ocar.opportunity: Dense synaptic reconstruction of a vertebrate whole brain has lagged invertebrate connectomes. Larval zebrafish at 5 days postfertilization is comparable in size to adult Drosophila, and the same animal can be imaged for function with two-photon calcium imaging before EM.
ocar.challenge: Synapse-level maps need both high-resolution whole-brain EM and tools to trace neuronal processes and detect chemical synapses at scale, plus checks against independent TEM and light-microscopic reconstructions.
ocar.action: Svara, Förster, Kubo, Januszewski, dal Maschio, Schubert, Kornfeld, Wanner, Laurell, Denk, and Baier in Nature Methods (2022) sectioned and imaged a larval zebrafish brain by serial block-face EM at 14 × 14 × 25 nm³ voxels, segmented with flood-filling networks, automated chemical-synapse detection, and stored neurons and connections in a queryable digital address book. They reconstructed a 208-neuron visual-motion network, mostly in pretectum, that had been functionally characterized in the same specimen, and mapped all 407 pre- and postsynaptic partners of two superficial interneurons in the tectum.
ocar.resolution: The resource provides automated neuron segmentation, synapse detection validated against TEM images and light-microscopic reconstructions, and example circuit reconstructions for visual motion processing. The authors present it as a foundation for synaptic-resolution analyses of the zebrafish nervous system.
ocar.future_work: Further proofreading and expansion of the address book, and broader structure–function circuits beyond the 208-neuron and two-SIN examples, are the implied uses of the resource.

summaries.beginner: The baby zebrafish brain is small enough to photograph entirely in an electron microscope, and the same fish can first be watched while it sees motion. This resource traces cells and synapses in that whole brain and works out a motion-processing circuit whose activity had already been recorded.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2022), Svara, Denk, Baier and colleagues publish a serial block-face EM volume of a larval zebrafish brain at 14 × 14 × 25 nm³, segmented with flood-filling networks and automated chemical-synapse detection. Neurons and connections are stored in a queryable address book. They reconstruct 208 neurons of a visual-motion network, mostly pretectal, previously characterized by two-photon calcium imaging in the same specimen, and enumerate all 407 synaptic partners of two tectal superficial interneurons. Validation includes TEM and light-microscopic comparisons.
summaries.advanced: This is a whole-brain imaging and segmentation resource, not a fully proofread vertebrate connectome comparable to C. elegans. Voxel size is anisotropic (25 nm in z). The 208-neuron and 407-partner analyses are targeted circuits, not a census of every cell. Same-animal calcium imaging covers the motion-processing example; the extracted text does not claim brain-wide functional registration. Proofreading-server simulations appear as extended data, indicating remaining infrastructure load.

plain_language_summary: The baby zebrafish brain is small enough to photograph entirely in an electron microscope, and the same fish can first be watched while it sees motion. This resource traces cells and synapses in that whole brain and works out a motion-processing circuit whose activity had already been recorded.

ocar.opportunity: The human cerebral cortex has about 1000 times more neurons than mouse cortex, and transcriptomics has suggested a higher fraction of inhibitory interneurons, but whether local synaptic circuit architecture evolved accordingly was untested. Comparative synapse-resolution connectomics is required to ask whether mouse cortical circuits are a faithful stand-in for human.
ocar.challenge: Homology at ion channels, receptors, and broad cell classes has been taken to imply similar cortical circuits, yet inhibitory-to-excitatory balance—and its relevance to neuropsychiatric hypotheses—depends on actual wiring. Prior human synaptic studies often used epileptic tissue after long pharmacological treatment.
ocar.action: Loomba, Straehle, Gangadharan, Helmstaedter and colleagues in Science (2022) acquired 3D EM connectomes from nonepileptic neurosurgical access-path samples of human temporal, parietal, and frontal cortex, plus macaque temporal and parietal cortex, and compared them with five mouse cortical connectomes. They quantified cell-type composition, synaptic input onto pyramidal cells, and interneuron targeting preferences. Analyzed connectomes comprised a total of about 1.6 million synapses.
ocar.resolution: A about 2.5-fold increase in interneurons in macaque and human versus mouse did not produce a commensurate rise in inhibitory-versus-excitatory synaptic input onto pyramidal cells. Pyramidal cells received a modest increase from about 12,000 synaptic inputs in mouse to about 15,000 in human, not a gain matching threefold cortical thickening. Instead, bipolar-type interneuron-targeting interneurons expanded and became more selective, yielding about a 10-fold expanded interneuron-to-interneuron network in human cortex that is only sparsely present in mouse.
ocar.future_work: Whether this expanded I-to-I network arises from growth of existing types or new subtypes, and what it does in health and disease, is left as the next question.

summaries.beginner: Mouse and human cortices are built from similar parts, but the human version is far larger and has more inhibitory cells. This comparison of 3D electron-microscope wiring finds that pyramidal cells still get a similar mix of excitation and inhibition; what grows instead is a network of inhibitory cells talking mainly to other inhibitory cells.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2022), Loomba, Helmstaedter and colleagues compare 3D EM connectomes from mouse (five datasets), macaque (two individuals, temporal and parietal), and human (two individuals, temporal, parietal, and frontal nonepileptic surgical tissue). Human/macaque cortex shows an about 2.5-fold expansion of interneurons versus mouse without a matching shift in I/E input balance onto pyramidal cells (~12,000 inputs in mouse versus ~15,000 in human). They report roughly a 10-fold expansion of an interneuron-to-interneuron network driven by bipolar-type, interneuron-preferring cells. About 1.6 million synapses were analyzed.
summaries.advanced: The extracted PDF body for this record is a different paper (Zhang et al. RegInpaint); pedagogical text follows the bibliographic abstract. Human samples are neurosurgical access-path tissue, not population-normal brains, though chosen to avoid epilepsy-surgery pharmacology. “About 10-fold” I-to-I expansion and 12,000 versus 15,000 inputs are abstract-level summaries. Whether new interneuron subtypes appear is explicitly unanswered. Last-common-ancestor times (~100 million years mouse–human; ~20 million years macaque–human) are evolutionary framing, not measured here.

plain_language_summary: Mouse and human cortices are built from similar parts, but the human version is far larger and has more inhibitory cells. This comparison of 3D electron-microscope wiring finds that pyramidal cells still get a similar mix of excitation and inhibition; what grows instead is a network of inhibitory cells talking mainly to other inhibitory cells.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic-resolution EM datasets and annotation methods have advanced rapidly, making larger and more complete insect connectomes practical. Matching neurons across datasets and to gene expression, activity, behavior, and development now lets researchers test circuit-function hypotheses.
ocar.challenge: Despite automation, false merges and missed branches still require proofreading. For an adult Drosophila central brain (~40,000 neurons) that effort has fallen from on the order of 2,000 to about 30 person-years, which remains a major coordinated campaign. Comparative questions—what is stereotyped versus variable across individuals, sexes, experience, development, and species—need multiple complete maps.
ocar.action: Galili, Jefferis, and Costa review in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2022) Drosophila connectomics progress, emphasizing adult datasets, sample preparation, ssTEM and FIB-SEM, alignment, automated segmentation and synapse detection, and proofreading communities. They survey what reconstructed neurons enable (NBLAST typing, input/output weights, NeuronBridge driver lines, motifs, cross-dataset comparison, modeling, axon–dendrite splits, neurotransmitter prediction) and summarize circuit insights in learned and innate olfaction, navigation, and sexual behavior.
ocar.resolution: Connectomics has revealed interconnected modules with hierarchical structure, recurrence, and integration of sensory streams in those behaviors. The hemibrain dense connectome provided instant access to a finished partial adult female brain and comparisons across individuals and three hemispheres. The authors argue that comparing connectomes to separate robust from variable features, and extending comparative connectomics across development, experience, sex, and species, will tightly link connectivity to function.
ocar.future_work: Forthcoming dense male and female VNC reconstructions and broader inter-individual comparisons are highlighted as near-term resources.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brain maps are now being finished fast enough that biologists can look up a cell, see who it connects to, and tie that wiring to smell, navigation, or courtship. This review explains how those maps are made, what you can do with a reconstructed neuron, and why comparing several brains is the next step.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Insect Science (2022), Galili, Jefferis, and Costa review Drosophila EM connectomics, from larval L1 CNS through adult hemibrain, FAFB, and emerging VNCs. They report that proofreading a ~40,000-neuron central brain dropped from order 2,000 to ~30 person-years, still requiring dedicated teams. The review catalogs analysis recipes (NBLAST, NeuronBridge, motif search, natverse axon–dendrite splits, neurotransmitter prediction) and argues that hierarchical, recurrent, multisensory modules already explain several behaviors, while comparative connectomics will separate stereotypy from variability.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinionated review with some personal-communication dataset timelines that may have shifted after 2022. Person-year figures are order-of-magnitude community estimates. Circuit claims about olfaction, navigation, and sexual behavior summarize cited studies, not new reconstructions here. “Finished insect connectome” for hemibrain refers to a dense partial female brain, not the entire CNS.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brain maps are now being finished fast enough that biologists can look up a cell, see who it connects to, and tie that wiring to smell, navigation, or courtship. This review explains how those maps are made, what you can do with a reconstructed neuron, and why comparing several brains is the next step.

ocar.opportunity: The octopus vertical lobe (VL) mediates long-term memory acquisition in a behaviorally advanced mollusk, but its synaptic architecture had not been reconstructed. A connectome of even a small VL volume could show whether this memory network uses the same motifs as cerebellum or mushroom body, or a different solution.
ocar.challenge: Prior views treated VL amacrine cells as a homogeneous population. Without EM, cell types, modulatory components, and synaptic motifs—and whether learning could be implemented with strictly feedforward flow—were unknown.
ocar.action: Bidel, Meirovitch, Schalek, Lu, Pavarino, Yang, Peleg, Wu, Shomrat, Berger, Shaked, Lichtman, and Hochner in eLife (2023) analyze a serial-section EM volume of Octopus vulgaris VL. They distinguish simple amacrine cells (SAMs) from a newly described complex amacrine type (CAMs), map SFL sensory-input axons, and relate a large bouton synapse to a previously identified LTP “memory site.”
ocar.resolution: Sensory input arrives via ~1.8 × 10⁶ axons that sparsely innervate two parallel, interconnected feedforward AM networks. SAMs are 89.3% of the ~25 × 10⁶ VL cells; each receives input from only a single SFL axon on a non-bifurcating primary neurite, implying each input neuron is represented in only ~12 ± 3.4 SAMs, with large boutons sparsely placed (1.03 ± 0.73 per 100 µm). CAMs are 1.6% of VL cells and integrate multiple inputs from axons and SAMs. The authors interpret SAMs as feeding sparse memorizable representations to the output layer and CAMs as monitoring global activity to supply balancing inhibition that sharpens stimulus-specific output—associative learning based strictly on feedforward flow.
ocar.future_work: The volume is a pioneering VL fragment; extending the census across the whole lobe and testing the proposed SAM/CAM computational roles physiologically are the next steps.

summaries.beginner: Octopuses learn using a brain area called the vertical lobe, whose wiring had never been mapped in detail. Electron-microscope reconstruction shows two kinds of small cells: a huge crowd that each hear from just one incoming cable, and a rarer type that listens more broadly and may sharpen the memory signal.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2023), Bidel, Meirovitch, Lichtman, Hochner and colleagues present the first EM connectomic analysis of a volume of Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe. About 1.8 million SFL axons sparsely innervate SAM and CAM amacrine networks among ~25 million VL cells (89.3% SAMs; 1.6% CAMs). Each SAM gets a single SFL synapse on an unbranched neurite (~12 ± 3.4 SAMs per input axon; 1.03 ± 0.73 large boutons per 100 µm), a site endowed with LTP. CAMs integrate multiple axon and SAM inputs. The authors propose a strictly feedforward memory architecture that still shares some morphological motifs with cerebellum and mushroom body.
summaries.advanced: Counts such as 1.8 million axons and 25 million VL cells are lobe-scale estimates combined with local EM, not a complete lobe reconstruction. The one-to-one SAM innervation inference assumes the sampled pattern holds tract-wide and that SFL axons rarely bifurcate. CAM computational “sharpening” is an interpretation from anatomy plus prior LTP physiology, not a new behavioral lesion test. Comparison to cerebellum and mushroom body is qualitative.

plain_language_summary: Octopuses learn using a brain area called the vertical lobe, whose wiring had never been mapped in detail. Electron-microscope reconstruction shows two kinds of small cells: a huge crowd that each hear from just one incoming cable, and a rarer type that listens more broadly and may sharpen the memory signal.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy already delivers nanometer-scale 3D structure from tissues, but conventional microscope throughput has limited both the size and the number of samples. Method innovations are now making whole organs and small organisms structurally imageable.
ocar.challenge: Faster acquisition shifts bottlenecks onto sample preparation, image analysis, and data management. Automatic segmentation and server-based annotation have progressed, yet several challenges in those downstream stages remain.
ocar.action: Kievits, Lane, Carroll, and Hoogenboom review in Journal of Microscopy (2022) recent trends in volume EM, emerging routes to higher throughput (including multi-beam SEM), and implications for preparation, analysis, and data handling. They place current practice in a lineage from 1940s TEM protocols and 1950s serial-section TEM through computer-assisted reconstruction.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that acquisition gains are driving a volume-EM revolution while stressing remaining pipeline bottlenecks, and it surveys how automatic segmentation and shared annotation tools have changed analysis even as data-management and preparation constraints grow.
ocar.future_work: Sustained progress will require matching sample-preparation, analysis, and storage methods to the new acquisition rates rather than treating imaging speed as the sole remaining problem.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can show tissue in three dimensions at nanometer detail, but they used to be too slow for whole organs. This review explains newer, faster microscopes and warns that preparing samples, analyzing the pictures, and storing the data become the new traffic jams.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Microscopy (2022), Kievits, Lane, Carroll, and Hoogenboom review methodology innovations for volume EM. They argue that throughput limits of conventional instruments are being lifted enough to image whole organs and small organisms, which in turn stresses sample preparation, image analysis, and data management. They highlight automatic segmentation and server-based annotation as rapidly advancing, while listing remaining challenges and emerging acquisition methods such as multi-beam SEM.
summaries.advanced: This is an invited methods review, not a new instrument or dataset. Claims about whole-organ imaging cite the field’s trajectory rather than a single benchmark in this paper. J. P. Hoogenboom discloses co-founding Delmic, which sells integrated microscopes including FAST-EM; readers should treat commercial mentions in that light. No quantitative throughput table is given in the extracted text.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can show tissue in three dimensions at nanometer detail, but they used to be too slow for whole organs. This review explains newer, faster microscopes and warns that preparing samples, analyzing the pictures, and storing the data become the new traffic jams.

ocar.opportunity: Dense maps that name cells, their subcellular parts, and their connections would reveal circuit principles, but annotating the vast number of objects in neuropil is the bottleneck even after nanometer-scale EM and automated instance segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Supervised networks for cell-fragment annotation need large labeled sets and do not transfer easily across tasks. Many reconstructed neurites in current volumes are truncated at the imaging boundary, so type inference from short fragments is especially valuable.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Li, Januszewski, Berger, Maitin-Shepard, Bodor, Collman, Schneider-Mizell, da Costa, Lichtman, and Jain introduce SegCLR in Nature Methods (2023): segmentation-guided contrastive learning of representations from 3D imagery and segmentations, applied to human and mouse cortical volumes. They train without per-task labels, then use lightweight classifiers on the embeddings.
ocar.resolution: SegCLR enabled accurate classification of cellular subcompartments and matched a supervised approach while requiring 400-fold fewer labeled examples. Cell types could be inferred from fragments as small as 10 μm. Applications include exploring layer 5 pyramidal subtypes and automated large-scale synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex. Embeddings, code, and pretrained weights are released.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize fragment typing for incomplete reconstructions and invite community use of the released human and mouse embedding datasets.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored in the cells in a 3D brain picture, it still does not know what part of a cell it is looking at or what cell type it is. This method learns a compact description of each snippet from the pictures themselves, so a few human labels can name parts and types even on very short broken pieces.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2023), Dorkenwald, Li, Jain and colleagues present SegCLR, a self-supervised contrastive method that embeds cells from 3D EM imagery plus segmentations. On human and mouse cortex it classifies subcompartments at supervised-level performance with 400-fold fewer labels and infers cell type from fragments as small as 10 μm. They demonstrate layer 5 pyramidal subtype exploration and automated synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex, and they release embeddings and code. A linear classifier on embeddings trains in minutes on one CPU with a few hundred labels, versus GPU-days for prior deep networks on related tasks.
summaries.advanced: Equivalence to supervised performance is for the subcompartment task with 400-fold fewer labels, not every possible annotation layer. The 10 μm fragment result is a reported operating point, not a guarantee on all morphologies. Large-scale partner analysis and L5 subtype exploration are demonstrations on the published volumes. Self-supervision still depends on the quality of the input segmentation.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored in the cells in a 3D brain picture, it still does not know what part of a cell it is looking at or what cell type it is. This method learns a compact description of each snippet from the pictures themselves, so a few human labels can name parts and types even on very short broken pieces.

ocar.opportunity: EM and deep learning now yield connectomes with tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of connections that interest non-specialists, not only the reconstructing lab. Publication of a paper is not enough: the data must be queryable in a browser and by APIs without downloading entire graphs.
ocar.challenge: Earlier reconstructions were small enough for experts to download. New graphs break that model; performance, public query languages, and reconstruction-quality checks become first-class requirements. Hosting such data online also has real cost.
ocar.action: Plaza, Clements, Dolafi, Umayam, Neubarth, Scheffer, and Berg introduce neuPrint in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022): a web interface for typical biological queries plus programmer APIs, with reconstruction-quality features. Internally, connectome data are a graph in neo4j, queried with Cypher. The paper also analyzes preprint versus journal-publication usage as an open-science experiment.
ocar.resolution: NeuPrint made Janelia FlyEM-style connectomes usable from a browser worldwide. The authors find that a significant fraction of readers proceed to examine the data directly; preprint posting triggered data inquiries and PDF downloads immediately, with little change at formal publication, implying many users wanted the data more than the narrative. They also report that keeping data available online imposes substantial additional costs on connectomics research.
ocar.future_work: The graph-in-neo4j design is argued to extend to still larger databases; sustaining public hosting and documentation is an ongoing operational challenge.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram with tens of millions of connections is useless to most scientists if they have to download a giant file. neuPrint is a website and programming interface that lets anyone ask ordinary biology questions of a connectome in a web browser.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), Plaza, Scheffer, Berg and colleagues present neuPrint, combining a browser UI, APIs, and quality-assessment tools over connectomes stored as neo4j graphs queried with Cypher. The system targets EM reconstructions with tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of synapses. Analyzing their own usage, they report that preprints drove immediate data access largely unaffected by later formal publication, and that public online hosting adds substantial cost. Code repositories for HTTP, Python, and related clients are cited.
summaries.advanced: Performance claims are qualitative (“typical queries”) without latency benchmarks in the extracted text. The open-science usage analysis is of this project’s readership, not a general trial of all data journals. neo4j/Cypher will not automatically solve every motif query at future scales. Organism is unspecified in the abstract; the motivating deployment is Janelia FlyEM connectomes.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram with tens of millions of connections is useless to most scientists if they have to download a giant file. neuPrint is a website and programming interface that lets anyone ask ordinary biology questions of a connectome in a web browser.

ocar.opportunity: Physiology can be measured in many animals, but synaptic structure is usually mapped with low throughput, blocking studies of how circuit variation relates to behavior. EM yields dense connectomes slowly; light microscopy is high-throughput and molecularly specific but historically lacked synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: That methodological gulf leaves individual differences, sex differences, and experience-dependent rewiring hard to quantify at single synapses across many animals.
ocar.action: Lillvis, Otsuna, Ding, Pisarev, Kawase, Colonell, Rokicki, Goina, Gao, Hu, Wang, Bogovic, Milkie, Meienberg, Mensh, Boyden, Saalfeld, Tillberg, and Dickson in eLife (2022) combine tissue expansion with lattice light-sheet microscopy (ExLLSM) and a high-throughput analysis pipeline to reconstruct selected Drosophila circuits at single-synapse resolution with molecular contrast. Protocols allow one sample to be prepared and analyzed within a week and several samples in parallel; software is released.
ocar.resolution: In Drosophila the method yielded synaptic counts similar to EM, enabled comparison of synaptic connectivity across sex and experience, and could correlate structural connectivity, functional connectivity, and behavior in the same animal. The authors argue it fills a gap for studying variability within and between species using relatively affordable microscopes.
ocar.future_work: Better fluorescent continuity for automated single-neuron (not just cell-type) segmentation, denser labeling, and genetic reagents for specific chemical and electrical synapse components are identified as next developments; the pipeline is intended to transfer where neurons can be labeled and tissue expanded.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes map every synapse but too slowly to compare many animals. This method swells the tissue, photographs it with a light-sheet microscope, and counts synapses in chosen fly circuits fast enough to compare sex, experience, and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2022), Lillvis, Tillberg, Dickson and colleagues present an ExLLSM pipeline for rapid, targeted synaptic reconstruction. Using Drosophila, they report synapse counts similar to EM, comparisons across sex and experience, and correlation of structure, function, and behavior in the same animal. A sample can be prepared and analyzed within a week and multiplexed; 8× expansion is discussed in the context of light-sheet imaging. Software tools for multi-terabyte volumes are released. Other light-sheet microscopes besides LLSM can image the expanded samples.
summaries.advanced: “Similar to EM” synaptic counts are a validation claim for selected Drosophila circuits, not a dense whole-brain connectome. Current analysis is largely at cell-type rather than fully automated single-cell resolution, as the authors note. Transfer to nematodes, rodents, zebrafish, and organoids is prospective, based on existing expansion and labeling literature. CNN synapse/neuron models may need retraining for new species.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes map every synapse but too slowly to compare many animals. This method swells the tissue, photographs it with a light-sheet microscope, and counts synapses in chosen fly circuits fast enough to compare sex, experience, and behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping networks from 3D EM still struggles with thin axons. Even strong automated segmentations usually need human proofreading before they support more demanding connectomic analyses.
ocar.challenge: Analyses differ in required error-free path length: local synaptic configurations may need only ~10 µm of axon, whereas neuron-to-neuron cortical connectomes need an additional order of magnitude of faithful axonal reconstruction, which has not been fully automatic.
ocar.action: Schmidt, Motta, Sievers, and Helmstaedter introduce RoboEM in Nature Methods (2024): an AI self-steering 3D flight system trained to navigate along neurites from EM alone. Applied to mouse and human cortical 3D-EM, it is used as automated proofreading to improve state-of-the-art segmentations, including flood-filling-network outputs.
ocar.resolution: RoboEM substantially improved automated segmentations and could replace manual proofreading for more complex connectomic analysis problems, with computational annotation cost for cortical connectomes about 400-fold lower than manual error correction. Split reduction was 3.5-fold better than state-of-the-art FFN agglomeration. The authors estimate that soma-seeded iterative use could extend fully automated axon reconstruction by multiple millimeters per neuron in petascale volumes. Compute cost increased by less than 2× in the discussed setting.
ocar.future_work: They argue RoboEM makes fully automated cortical connectomes at the scale of thousands to ten thousand neurons plausible by focusing on long, locally thin axons.

summaries.beginner: Computers still lose thin axons in 3D electron-microscope volumes, so people spend huge effort correcting maps. RoboEM is a virtual pilot that flies along those axons from the pictures alone, fixing breaks cheaply enough that much of that human proofreading can be skipped.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2024), Schmidt, Motta, Sievers, and Helmstaedter present RoboEM, a self-steering 3D flight tracer using only EM as input. On mouse and human cortex it improves automated segmentations and can replace manual proofreading for more complex analyses, with about 400-fold lower computational annotation cost than manual correction and 3.5-fold better split reduction than FFN agglomeration. Calibration used volumes around 100–150 µm on a side; projections to millimeter axons in petascale data are estimated from soma-seeded iterative application.
summaries.advanced: The 400-fold cost figure compares computational annotation to manual error correction for cortical connectomes as stated by the authors, not wall-clock of a whole pipeline. Performance on 100–150 µm cubes is measured; millimeter-to-centimeter axon claims are estimates. FFN similarity is discussed: RoboEM traces centerlines with “growth inertia,” which the authors say solves problems volume methods miss. It does not eliminate all human work for every analysis type.

plain_language_summary: Computers still lose thin axons in 3D electron-microscope volumes, so people spend huge effort correcting maps. RoboEM is a virtual pilot that flies along those axons from the pictures alone, fixing breaks cheaply enough that much of that human proofreading can be skipped.

ocar.opportunity: Knowing network architecture is essential for understanding brain function. Drosophila larva offers rich behavior—learning, value computation, action selection—in a brain small enough for a complete synaptic-resolution map.
ocar.challenge: Without a whole-brain synapse-level connectome, claims about hubs, feedback, multisensory integration, and resemblance to machine-learning architectures remain incomplete. Axon versus dendrite compartmentalization also changes how connections should be counted.
ocar.action: Winding, Pedigo, Barnes, Patsolic, Park, Kazimiers, Fushiki, Andrade, Khandelwal, Valdes-Aleman, Li, Randel, Barsotti, Correia, Fetter, Hartenstein, Priebe, Vogelstein, Cardona, and Zlatic in Science (2023) map the synaptic-resolution connectome of an entire Drosophila larva brain. They split each neuron into axon and dendrite, yielding four connection types, cluster neurons from connectivity, and track polysynaptic pathways from synapse numbers.
ocar.resolution: The reconstruction comprises 3,016 neurons and 548,000 synapses. Connectivity clustering yielded 93 neuron types with internally consistent morphology and, where known, function. Most connections were axon-to-dendrite (66.4%), with axon-to-axon 26.4%, dendrite-to-dendrite 5.4%, and dendrite-to-axon 1.8%; noncanonical types were pronounced in learning and action-selection circuits. The authors report pervasive multisensory and interhemispheric integration, high recurrence, abundant feedback from descending neurons, and novel motifs; the most recurrent circuits involved learning-center input and output neurons. Some structural features resembled powerful machine-learning architectures (multilayer shortcuts, nested recurrent loops).
ocar.future_work: The map is offered as a basis for experimental and theoretical circuit studies; many connectivity-defined clusters still lack gene-expression and functional characterization.

summaries.beginner: This paper maps every neuron and synapse in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain. The wiring is highly recurrent, mixes the senses, and uses extra connection styles beyond the usual axon-to-dendrite pattern, especially in the learning center.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2023), Winding, Pedigo, Cardona, Zlatic and colleagues report a complete Drosophila larva brain connectome of 3,016 neurons and 548,000 synapses. Neurons were split into axon and dendrite compartments (four connection types). Unbiased connectivity clustering produced 93 types. Architecture analysis finds widespread multisensory and interhemispheric integration, recurrence concentrated at learning-center input/output neurons, descending-neuron feedback, and motifs including multilayer shortcuts and nested loops. Axon–axon connections are 26.4% of synapses and are discussed in the context of mushroom-body teaching signals and possible lateral inhibition.
summaries.advanced: Abstract and PDF neuron/synapse totals differ slightly (3,013 / 544,000 versus 3,016 / 548,000); figures here follow the reconstructed PDF. “Entire insect brain” is the larva CNS brain, not adult Drosophila. Functional interpretations of a-a synapses (e.g., inhibitory mAChR-B) draw on adult literature. Clustering by connectivity is one type definition; many clusters remain uncharacterized. Machine-learning architecture resemblance is analogical.

plain_language_summary: This paper maps every neuron and synapse in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain. The wiring is highly recurrent, mixes the senses, and uses extra connection styles beyond the usual axon-to-dendrite pattern, especially in the learning center.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic wiring diagrams miss extrasynaptic neuropeptide signaling, which is widespread and essential in all nervous systems. C. elegans offers single-cell anatomy, gene expression, and a growing biochemical map of peptide–receptor pairs, so a draft peptidergic connectome is feasible.
ocar.challenge: Neuropeptidergic networks are largely uncharacterized as graphs. Diffusion range is uncertain, many receptors remain orphan, and topology may differ radically from synaptic networks.
ocar.action: Ripoll-Sánchez, Watteyne, Sun, Fernandez, Taylor, Weinreb, Hammarlund, Miller, Hobert, Beets, Vértes, and Schafer in Neuron (2023) integrate GPCR deorphanization (51 GPCRs, 49 neuropeptide precursors, 92 ligand–receptor pairs), scRNA-seq of 302 neurons, and anatomical contacts to build a draft C. elegans neuropeptide connectome. They analyze density, cascades, autocrine foci, communities, hubs, and rich-club structure under conservative diffusion assumptions.
ocar.resolution: The peptidergic network is over 10-fold denser than the synaptic connectome even with conservative diffusion assumptions. It is decentralized, with a large interconnected core of three communities sharing similar input patterns. Several of the most important nodes are little-studied neurons specialized for peptidergic neuromodulation. Degree correlates with synaptic degree (r = 0.54, p = 3.1e−14). A rich club of 156 neurons is reported for the short-range model (166 for mid-range).
ocar.future_work: The authors anticipate this draft as a prototype for organizational principles of neuroendocrine networks; additional deorphanization and spatial diffusion measurements would refine edges.

summaries.beginner: Worms—and likely all brains—send many messages not across tight synapses but as chemical broadcasts. This paper draws a first whole-animal map of those peptide signals and finds a dense, less hub-dominated network than the classic synaptic wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2023), Ripoll-Sánchez, Beets, Vértes, Schafer and colleagues assemble a draft C. elegans neuropeptidergic connectome from 51 GPCRs, 49 peptide genes, 92 validated pairs, and expression in 302 neurons. Even under conservative diffusion assumptions the graph is over 10-fold denser than the synaptic connectome, with extended cascades, autocrine foci, and a decentralized core of three input-similarity communities. Hubs include little-studied peptidergic specialists. Synaptic and peptidergic degrees correlate (r = 0.54); a short-range rich club contains 156 neurons.
summaries.advanced: Edges are model-based (expression × biochemically validated pairs × assumed range), not imaged peptide release. Conservative diffusion still yields >10× density; true range could change topology. Orphan receptors and peptides are missing by construction. Correlation r = 0.54 leaves much unmatched variance between synaptic and peptidergic importance. Behavioral examples (e.g., FLP-20) illustrate timescales, not a full functional validation of the graph.

plain_language_summary: Worms—and likely all brains—send many messages not across tight synapses but as chemical broadcasts. This paper draws a first whole-animal map of those peptide signals and finds a dense, less hub-dominated network than the classic synaptic wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: Human association cortex is rarely available as rapidly preserved, high-quality tissue for nanometer-scale circuit reconstruction. A cubic-millimeter, full-thickness volume would let researchers see all layers, white matter, and intra-cortical axons that may travel over a hundred microns before the first synapse.
ocar.challenge: Access, preservation, petascale imaging, and automated segmentation with remaining split/merge errors all stand between a surgical sample and a usable human cortical connectome. Epilepsy history and medications are additional confounds even when the resected piece is “in the way” rather than the focus of disease.
ocar.action: Shapson-Coe, Januszewski, Berger, Pope, Wu, Blakely, Schalek, Li, Wang, Maitin-Shepard, Karlupia, Dorkenwald, Jain, Lichtman and colleagues (bioRxiv 2021) rapidly preserved a human temporal-lobe surgical sample, stained ~1 mm³, cut more than 5,000 slices at ~30 nm, and imaged with multibeam SEM. Computational reconstruction yielded 57,216 cells, hundreds of millions of neurites, and 133.7 million synapses in a 1.4-petabyte volume; 104 cells were manually proofread. Data are available to browse online.
ocar.resolution: Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1, with oligodendrocytes the most common cell type. Excitatory spiny neurons were 69% of neurons; excitatory synapses 76%. Synaptic drive onto spiny neurons was 70% excitatory versus 48% onto inhibitory interneurons. Despite incomplete automated segmentation, validated connections could be generated among most excitatory and inhibitory types within and between layers. Deep-layer excitatory cells split into new structural/connectivity subsets; chandelier cells innervated one another’s axon initial segments as well as those of excitatory neurons. Rare axons made up to ~20 synapses onto a target, among thousands of weak inputs, suggesting outsized influence.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that rapid immersion of fresh tissue can match perfusion quality and that further scale-up toward mouse-brain-scale volumes is becoming realistic; interpreting findings in light of possible epilepsy-related or pharmacological effects remains necessary.

summaries.beginner: A cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex was sliced thousands of times, photographed with a fast electron microscope, and reconstructed into a digital tissue with tens of thousands of cells and more than a hundred million synapses. Among many findings, glia outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Shapson-Coe, Januszewski, Jain, Lichtman and colleagues reconstruct a 1 mm³ human temporal-cortex sample: >5,000 sections at ~30 nm, 1.4 PB, 57,216 cells, 133.7 million synapses, and 104 manually proofread cells. Glia:neuron is 2:1; oligodendrocytes are most common; 69% of neurons are excitatory spiny cells; 76% of synapses are excitatory (70% of synapses onto spiny neurons versus 48% onto interneurons). They describe new deep-layer excitatory subsets, chandelier-to-chandelier AIS innervation, and rare multi-synaptic axons (up to ~20 contacts). Online browsing of the H01 volume is provided.
summaries.advanced: Automated segmentation is explicitly incomplete (splits/merges). The donor had epilepsy; the sample was access-path tissue judged not primarily pathological, but pharmacology and disease effects cannot be excluded. 1 mm³ is argued as sufficient for layer-spanning local circuits, not a whole area. Multi-synaptic “powerful” inputs are anatomical multiplicity, not measured EPSP amplitude. Comparison to a 2015 mouse saturated reconstruction is a scale-up narrative (~4 years, ~660,000-fold voxels), not a matched biology study.

plain_language_summary: A cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex was sliced thousands of times, photographed with a fast electron microscope, and reconstructed into a digital tissue with tens of thousands of cells and more than a hundred million synapses. Among many findings, glia outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous-system organization spans synapses, neuronal morphology, and brain-region connectivity, but a complete structure–function model integrated across those scales had not been achieved even in a small animal. C. elegans offers a compact nerve ring plus existing synaptic and gap-junction connectomes.
ocar.challenge: The nerve ring was long treated as a densely packed process tract without an internal spatial model that could explain which synapses are possible. Connectomes were often treated as invariant, hiding core versus variable wiring.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen in Nature (2021) integrate volumetric reconstructions of the nerve ring from two animals with corresponding chemical-synapse and gap-junction connectomes. They analyze local neighborhoods, variability versus a core circuit, and propose a modular structure–function architecture.
ocar.resolution: Local neighborhoods spatially constrain and support the synaptic connectome. The C. elegans connectome is not invariant: a precisely wired core is embedded in variable connectivity, from which they derive a candidate reference core connectome. On that reference they propose modules supporting sensory computation and integration, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination, arguing these are scalable, robust features that may be universal across phyla.
ocar.future_work: The model is a template for asking which spatial and modular principles generalize; more animals would better separate core from variable edges.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s central nerve bundle was thought to be a packed tangle of wires. Reconstructing it in 3D in two animals shows orderly neighborhoods, a shared core circuit, and extra connections that differ between individuals.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen present a structure–function model of the C. elegans nerve ring from two complete volumetric reconstructions aligned to synaptic and gap-junction connectomes.
