They show internal spatial neighborhoods that constrain synapses, reject strict invariance in favor of a core circuit plus variable background, and propose a modular architecture for sensory integration, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination.
summaries.advanced: n = 2 animals limits statistical separation of core versus variable synapses. Universality across phyla is an interpretive claim. Gap junctions are included in the integrated model but chemical-synapse analyses dominate many narratives of variability. The extracted PDF is an accepted manuscript with figure placeholders; quantitative neighborhood statistics are not in the truncated text beyond the abstract-level findings.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s central nerve bundle was thought to be a packed tangle of wires. Reconstructing it in 3D in two animals shows orderly neighborhoods, a shared core circuit, and extra connections that differ between individuals.

ocar.opportunity: EM can reconstruct circuits at synaptic resolution, but cortical axons are morphologically hard and there was no public large-scale cortical EM dataset with dense axon instance ground truth for training and evaluation.
ocar.challenge: Broken membranes, tight axon bundles, invaginations, thin segments, and image defects cause merge and split errors. Without dense axon labels, methods cannot be compared at scale.
ocar.action: Wei, Lee, Li, Lu, Bae, Liu, Zhang, dos Santos, Lin, Uram, Wang, Arganda-Carreras, Matejek, Kasthuri, Lichtman, and Pfister introduce AxonEM at MICCAI (2021): two 30 × 30 × 30 µm³ EM volumes from human and mouse cortex with dense 3D axon instance segmentation. They proofread over 18,000 axon instances and densely annotate nine ground-truth subvolumes per volume for training, then reimplement affinity U-Net and flood-filling network baselines.
ocar.resolution: The dataset enables large-scale axon evaluation. Affinity U-Net expected run length reached 88% of ground truth on mouse (AxonEM-M) and 65% on human (AxonEM-H). An FFN baseline without the original multi-scale consensus and agglomeration steps was substantially worse (reported as 34% and 22% of GT ERL). Code and data are public.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the set to foster better axon methods and to serve as a testbed for other applications; a more faithful FFN baseline remains future work.

summaries.beginner: Thin axons in cortex are among the hardest objects to color in automatically, and there was no big public test set. AxonEM hands the community two cubes of human and mouse cortex with more than 18,000 carefully checked axons so algorithms can be scored fairly.
summaries.intermediate: In MICCAI (2021), Wei, Lee, Pfister and colleagues release AxonEM: two 30 × 30 × 30 µm³ cortical EM volumes (human and mouse) with dense proofreading of over 18,000 axons and nine densely annotated training subvolumes per volume. Reimplemented affinity U-Net agglomeration achieved axon expected run length of 88% of GT on mouse and 65% on human. A partial FFN reimplementation lagged (22–34% of GT ERL) because multi-scale consensus and FFN agglomeration were omitted. Data and code are at the Connectomics Bazaar AxonEM page.
summaries.advanced: Volumes are 30 µm cubes, not cortical columns. FFN numbers are not a reproduction of Januszewski et al.’s full pipeline; the authors warn against treating them as SOTA FFN performance. ERL percentages are relative to GT axon ERL in these volumes. Human versus mouse difficulty (65% vs 88%) should not be over-interpreted as a species law. Some authors disclose Zetta AI financial interests.

plain_language_summary: Thin axons in cortex are among the hardest objects to color in automatically, and there was no big public test set. AxonEM hands the community two cubes of human and mouse cortex with more than 18,000 carefully checked axons so algorithms can be scored fairly.

ocar.opportunity: As an animal grows, its nervous system and behaviors mature, but how much a complete brain’s wiring diagram remodels after birth was unknown. C. elegans is isogenic and small enough that full brains can be reconstructed at multiple ages.
ocar.challenge: Prior connectomes were essentially snapshots, so stable, variable, and developmental edges could not be separated. Gap-junction visibility and limited animals per stage further constrain developmental inference.
ocar.action: Witvliet, Mulcahy, Mitchell, Meirovitch, Berger, Wu, Liu, Koh, Parvathala, Holmyard, Schalek, Shavit, Chisholm, Lichtman, Samuel, and Zhen in Nature (2021) used serial-section EM to reconstruct the full brain of eight isogenic C. elegans individuals across postnatal stages. They compared geometry, chemical synapses among individuals, and consistent wiring changes across maturation.
ocar.resolution: Overall brain geometry is preserved from birth to adulthood, while chemical synaptic connectivity changes substantially on that scaffold. Individuals differ enough that each brain is partly unique, yet many neuron-pair changes are consistent across maturation, altering existing weights and adding connections. Central decision-making circuitry is maintained while sensory and motor pathways remodel; with age the brain becomes more feedforward and discernibly modular. Most connectivity asymmetry present at birth is eliminated during L1. Relative neurite-length proportions correlate between L1 and adult (Spearman r = 0.75, n = 947).
ocar.future_work: The authors note that gap junctions were not included at the same confidence, and that most time points have only one animal, so age-specific variability remains undersampled; higher throughput per stage is needed.

summaries.beginner: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), Witvliet, Lichtman, Samuel, Zhen and colleagues reconstruct complete brains of eight isogenic C. elegans across postnatal life. Geometry is stable while chemical synapses remodel: individual uniqueness plus stereotyped developmental additions and weight changes. Decision-making cores persist; sensory and motor pathways change more. Networks become more feedforward and modular with age. Left–right asymmetry and missing connections drop most during L1. An online database (nemanode.org) hosts the connectomes, including electrical synapses where visible.
summaries.advanced: Gap junctions are a stated limitation of the analysis. Typically one connectome per time point prevents measuring within-age variability. Chemical-synapse scoring is higher confidence than electrical. Isogenic animals reduce genetic noise but not all environmental or stochastic developmental effects. Spearman r = 0.75 describes relative neurite-length preservation, not synapse-by-synapse invariance.

plain_language_summary: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes list every synapse location and neuron shape, which might let researchers infer physiological connection weights and when axons versus dendrites must be modeled as separate compartments. Doing so requires pairing anatomy with subthreshold physiology on the same cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Network models often treat synaptic weights and compartmentalization as free parameters. Anatomy–physiology links known for one synapse type (for example mouse neocortex PSD size versus uEPSP) may not generalize across diverse neurons. Drosophila hemibrain offers morphological diversity but needs matched physiology.
ocar.action: Liu, Davoudian, Lizbinski, and Jeanne (bioRxiv 2021) compare anatomy and physiology at subcellular, subthreshold resolution in a stereotyped Drosophila olfactory network (projection neurons to lateral horn neurons). They relate synapse number, density, and location to somatic unitary EPSP amplitude and fit biophysical models of axonal versus dendritic integration.
ocar.resolution: Synapse density and location jointly predict the amplitude of the somatic postsynaptic potential evoked by a single presynaptic spike. Number of synapses and LHN surface area predict somatic uEPSPs for dendritic connections but severely underpredict when input is axonal. Models predict that electrical compartmentalization lets axon and dendrite arbors balance independent and interacting computations.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame this as a step from connectivity maps toward activity maps; testing whether the same anatomical predictors hold beyond PN–LHN pairs is the next generalization.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram says how many synapses two cells share, but not how strong the message feels. In the fly olfactory system, counting synapses and noting whether they sit on the dendrite or the axon predicts the electrical bump recorded at the cell body after one spike.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Liu, Davoudian, Lizbinski, and Jeanne pair Drosophila hemibrain-style anatomy with subthreshold physiology in olfactory projection-neuron to lateral-horn-neuron connections. Synapse density and location jointly predict somatic uEPSP amplitude from a single presynaptic spike. Dendritic connections are predicted by synapse number and LHN surface area; axonal input is not. Compartmental models indicate axons and dendrites can compute somewhat separately while still interacting.
summaries.advanced: Results are for a stereotyped olfactory subnetwork, not a brain-wide weight table. Predictors are of somatic uEPSP, which can miss local axonal computations the models themselves emphasize. Hemibrain anatomy is from published reconstructions, not necessarily the same individual as the physiology. No single scalar R² is given in the extracted text. Mouse PSD–uEPSP linearity is cited as motivation, not a result of this paper.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram says how many synapses two cells share, but not how strong the message feels. In the fly olfactory system, counting synapses and noting whether they sit on the dendrite or the axon predicts the electrical bump recorded at the cell body after one spike.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding the brain requires relating each neuron’s functional responses to the synaptic architecture that shapes them. Crick’s 1979 “impossible” request—a cubic millimeter with both wiring and firing—is now approachable by combining dense calcium imaging with volumetric EM.
ocar.challenge: Prior structure–function studies were fragmentary (single cells, slices, or viral tracing). Co-registering awake visual physiology with a millimeter-scale EM volume spanning multiple cortical areas, then proofreading enough axons to count thousands of cell-to-cell connections, is a massive alignment and reconstruction problem.
ocar.action: The MICrONS Consortium in Nature (2025) recorded activity from around 75,000 neurons in VISp, VISrl, VISal, and VISlm of an awake mouse viewing natural movies and synthetic stimuli, co-registered to an EM reconstruction with more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. Proofreading of a subset yielded complete dendritic trees plus local and inter-areal axons. They release the dataset and retrieval tools; accompanying papers analyze cell types, a cortical-column connectivity diagram, inhibitory motifs linked to gene expression, visual integration, neuronal invariances, and excitatory wiring within and across areas.
ocar.resolution: The resource includes Neuroglancer visualizations of proofread examples (layer 5 thick-tufted and near-projecting cells, layer 4, layer 2/3). Reporting materials specify a male Slc17a7-Cre × Ai162 mouse, IACUC approval at Allen Institute or Baylor, no experimental replication, and exclusion of neurons without proofread axons from a subset of analyses.
ocar.future_work: Continued proofreading is described as making the reconstruction increasingly accurate; accompanying papers are the venue for the biological conclusions built on this release.

summaries.beginner: A mouse watched movies while thousands of its visual-cortex cells lit up, and the same cubic millimeter was later reconstructed in an electron microscope with hundreds of millions of synapses. The public dataset lets anyone match those firing patterns to actual wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), the MICrONS Consortium releases a functional connectomics resource: dense two-photon calcium imaging of ~75,000 neurons across VISp and higher visual areas (VISrl, VISal, VISlm) in an awake mouse, co-registered with serial-section TEM of >200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. Proofread neurons include full dendrites and inter-areal axons with up to thousands of connections per cell. Companion papers address cell types, column connectivity, inhibitory motifs, visual computation, invariances, and excitatory wiring rules. Tools for retrieval and Neuroglancer viewing are included.
summaries.advanced: This is a resource-and-consortium paper; many biological claims are deferred to accompanying studies. n = 1 male mouse; reporting summary states no replication, randomization, or blinding. Functional sampling aimed to include primary and secondary visual areas rather than a pre-specified power calculation. Analyses that need axons exclude non-proofread neurons. Calcium imaging and EM co-registration inherit residual alignment error not quantified in the extracted text.

plain_language_summary: A mouse watched movies while thousands of its visual-cortex cells lit up, and the same cubic millimeter was later reconstructed in an electron microscope with hundreds of millions of synapses. The public dataset lets anyone match those firing patterns to actual wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Dopaminergic axons strongly influence behavior including addiction, but how they communicate in nucleus accumbens—point synapses versus volume transmission—and how that anatomy changes after cocaine remain poorly resolved at EM scale.
ocar.challenge: Light-level varicosity counts cannot show vesicles, synapses, spinules, or mitochondrial remodeling. Cell-type-specific EM labeling is needed to follow identified DA axons in large volumes before and after drug exposure.
ocar.action: Wildenberg, Sorokina, Koranda, Monical, Heer, Sheffield, Zhuang, McGehee, and Kasthuri in eLife (2021) combine genetic labeling (mito-Apex2 in DAT+ neurons) with large-volume serial EM of mouse NAc in controls and after a brief cocaine-sensitization protocol. They classify varicosities by vesicle content, score synapses versus spinule-like interdigitations, and quantify branching, glial ensheathment, bulbs, and mitochondrial length.
ocar.resolution: Individual DA axons contain mixed varicosity types that appear non-randomly ordered. Classic synapses were rare (<2%, 6/410), whereas spinule-like structures with neighbors were more common (15%, 61/410). Days after cocaine, DA axons were more branched, formed mitochondria-filled blind-ended bulbs, and were surrounded by elaborated glia. Mitochondrial length increased ~2.2-fold relative to control only in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites. The authors conclude NAc DA transmission is unlikely to be classical synaptic and that anatomical plasticity after cocaine is largely axonal rearrangement with correlated mitochondrial change.
ocar.future_work: Follow-up in self-administration or longer abstinence, and tests of whether DAT+ subclasses differ, are needed; the authors treat sensitization as a minimal acute model, not full addiction.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine cables in the mouse reward center almost never make textbook synapses. They more often interleave with neighbors and, after a short cocaine exposure, sprout extra branches and swollen, mitochondria-packed endings.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), Wildenberg, Kasthuri and colleagues reconstruct labeled dopaminergic axons in mouse nucleus accumbens with serial EM, with and without cocaine sensitization. Varicosity types differ by vesicle content and are non-randomly ordered along axons. Specific synapses were 6/410 (<2%); spinule-like interdigitations 61/410 (15%). After cocaine, axons branched more, formed mitochondria-filled bulbs, and attracted elaborated glia; mitochondrial length rose ~2.2× only in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites.
summaries.advanced: Synapse rarity is 6/410 scored varicosities in this labeled NAc sample, not all DA systems. Cocaine protocol is sensitization, which the authors distinguish from addiction models. Labeling uses DAT-driven AAV; subclass bias cannot be fully excluded despite matched virus batches. Mitochondrial 2.2× is a length increase in specified compartments, not a metabolic assay. Volume-transmission inference is from lack of synaptic specializations plus spinules, not measured extrasynaptic concentrations.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine cables in the mouse reward center almost never make textbook synapses. They more often interleave with neighbors and, after a short cocaine exposure, sprout extra branches and swollen, mitochondria-packed endings.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM has mapped invertebrate nervous systems but only small chunks of mammalian brain. Serial-section EM of a near cubic millimeter produces petascale images that need a computational pipeline for alignment, segmentation, semantics, and synapses.
ocar.challenge: Serial sections contain numerous cracks and folds, so alignment cannot assume smooth transforms. Boundary detection, semantic labeling (axon, dendrite, soma), synapse assignment, and agglomeration must run in distributed cloud workflows whose intermediates remain inspectable.
ocar.action: Macrina, Lee, Lu, Turner, Wu, Popovych, Silversmith, Kemnitz, Bae, Castro, Dorkenwald, Seung and the MICrONS consortium (bioRxiv 2021) describe a pipeline of convolutional nets for nonsmooth serial-section alignment, neuronal boundary detection, semantic voxel labels, and synapse detection/assignment, followed by mean-affinity agglomeration with semantic and size constraints. Intermediate results live in cloud storage as viewable images. They apply it to ~1.5 petapixels from a P87 male mouse spanning four visual cortical areas (Yin et al. 2020 acquisition).
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produced a public automated reconstruction of that multi-area visual-cortex volume, with publicly available code. Discussion emphasizes remaining errors at residual misalignments, mitochondria or ER contacting plasma membrane, low contrast, and missing/thick sections, and sketches scaling hierarchical agglomeration toward an exascale whole-mouse brain (~1000× larger).
ocar.future_work: Automated error detection/correction is cited as not yet deployed at scale in this pipeline; reducing cracks/folds in future acquisitions or considering block-face EM are discussed as complementary paths.

summaries.beginner: Photographing a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex on thousands of slices creates a mountain of images full of cracks and folds. This paper is the factory software that lines the slices up, finds cell borders and synapses, and glues fragments together in the cloud so people can browse an automated reconstruction.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Macrina, Lee, Lu, Turner, Seung and colleagues present automated methods for petascale serial-section EM reconstruction, applied to ~1.5 petapixels spanning four visual areas of a P87 male mouse (MICrONS). Convolutional nets estimate nonsmooth alignments through cracks and folds, detect membranes, assign semantic compartments, and detect synapses; mean-affinity agglomeration uses semantic and size constraints. Cloud-hosted intermediates aid debugging. Code and the reconstructed volume are public.
summaries.advanced: This paper is the methods companion to the MICrONS reconstruction, not a proofread connectome. Alignment errors still cause a significant fraction of segmentation mistakes. Hierarchical agglomeration’s top octree merge is called out as the operation that would need a ~100× larger shared-memory machine for a whole mouse brain unless redesigned. Competing block-face EM is discussed, not used. Comparison to Shapson-Coe human temporal cortex is size context only.

plain_language_summary: Photographing a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex on thousands of slices creates a mountain of images full of cracks and folds. This paper is the factory software that lines the slices up, finds cell borders and synapses, and glues fragments together in the cloud so people can browse an automated reconstruction.
